name: Breath strips

card.summary: Dissolving flavour films for a quick breath refresh; no trials on their effect.
card.note: Little published evidence specific to breath strips.

quick.overview:
Breath strips are thin films that dissolve on the tongue and release mint flavour.

No clinical studies of their effect on breath were found; the format itself comes from fast-dissolving drug films.
quick.mechanism: The film dissolves quickly and the flavour masks odour for a short time.
quick.risks: No specific risks are documented in the sources reviewed.

lead: Breath strips are thin, flavoured films that dissolve on the tongue within moments and are used to freshen breath. People carry them as a pocketable alternative to mints so that their breath smells fresher in close conversation, on dates or at work, which supports a more polished impression.[1]

They use fast-dissolving film technology, developed as an oral delivery format for drugs and described in pharmaceutical reviews as a very thin oral strip that disintegrates on the tongue, adopted partly to mask bitter tastes and improve user compliance.[1] Breath strips apply the same format to flavour delivery.[1]

Dentistry and medical references describe mints, gum and similar products as short-term masking of odour. Bad breath most often originates in the mouth, particularly the back of the tongue, where bacteria break down proteins and release foul-smelling gases; other sources include gum disease, tooth decay, trapped food and dentures that are not cleaned well.[2] Tongue cleaning, mouthwash and flossing are listed as initial steps for the cause.[2] No clinical trials of breath strips for breath odour were found.

chain: Flavour is released in the mouth
Breath smells fresher for a short time
angle.text: A strip placed on the tongue delivers flavour within seconds, giving fresher-smelling breath for a while. Users keep them for quick refreshes before talking closely with others.

infobox: Pocketable strips, often in a small dispenser

paras: A review of fast-dissolving films describes very thin oral strips that disintegrate on the tongue and were adopted partly to mask bitter tastes and improve user compliance.[1] Breath strips apply the same format to flavour delivery. Listerine's product range, for example, has included quick-dissolving strips.[3]

Wikipedia's halitosis article describes products such as mints and gum as masking measures that address the smell rather than its cause. It notes bad breath may be transient and often passes after eating, drinking, brushing, flossing or rinsing, and says evidence does not support benefit from dietary changes or chewing gum.[2]

Treatment depends on the cause; initial steps include tongue cleaning, mouthwash and flossing, with gum disease, cavities or other conditions treated where present. Evidence for specific mouthwashes and tongue cleaners is described as tentative.[2]
Patent applications describe confections, including dissolvable forms, that carry pH or buffering modifiers intended to raise the pH in the mouth by about one to two units.[4][5]
Strips are mentioned as a pocketable alternative to mints for brief breath freshening.
